module.title: Unit 4: Dilemmas: First & Second Conditional
module.objective: Mampu membicarakan situasi hipotetis, mengungkapkan keinginan, meminta maaf dan menerima permintaan maaf menggunakan first, second, dan third conditional dengan tepat

content.summary: Welcome to your fourth reading mission. In this module, you will explore how people navigate tricky moral choices and everyday dilemmas. You will learn to use the first conditional for realistic future possibilities and the second conditional for imaginary or unlikely situations, helping you discuss what you would do when faced with difficult decisions.

linguisticTarget.grammar: First Conditional (if + present simple, will + base verb) and Second Conditional (if + past simple, would + base verb).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Verbs and phrases related to honesty, dilemmas, owning up to mistakes, and making decisions.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for specific conditional outcomes and skimming paragraphs to identify the core moral dilemma.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas and arguments in short B2 texts about personal dilemmas.
Locate specific conditional structures and their logical outcomes in written passages.
Distinguish between real future possibilities and imaginary hypothetical scenarios.

contextWarmup.prompt: If you found a wallet full of cash on the street with no identification inside, what would you do first?
options: I would take it to the nearest police station immediately.
I will keep the money because nobody is watching me.
I am hiding the wallet under a bush and walking away.
contextWarmup.explanation: Option A uses the correct second conditional structure (would + base verb) to describe an imagined moral dilemma and an ethical response.

rules: First Conditional: Use 'if + present simple' in the condition clause and 'will + verb' in the result clause to talk about realistic future situations.
Second Conditional: Use 'if + past simple' in the condition clause and 'would + verb' in the result clause to talk about hypothetical or unlikely present and future situations.
Comma Placement: When the 'if' clause comes at the beginning of the sentence, separate it from the main clause with a comma.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mistakenly put 'would' inside the 'if' clause of a second conditional sentence, or use 'will' in the second conditional result clause.
commonTrap.wrong: If I would find £100, I will give it back.
commonTrap.correct: If I found £100, I would give it back.

paragraphs: Life is full of unexpected dilemmas that test our character. Imagine you are taking a crucial history exam and your best friend whispers an answer to you. If you accept the answer, you might get a top grade, but you will know you cheated. On the other hand, if you refuse the help, your friend might feel embarrassed or angry. Situations like this force us to make up our minds quickly and decide what matters more to us personal success or honesty.

Consider another common scenario involving damaged property. If someone accidentally broke a window at school and nobody saw them, they would face a tough choice. If they hide the truth, they might get away with it for a few days. However, if they own up to the mistake and tell the truth, they will earn the respect of their teachers. Most people agree that owning up is difficult, but it prevents guilt from building up over time.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Dilemmas and Conditional Structures

content.summary: Master writing about moral dilemmas, hypothetical scenarios, and conditional arguments using precise grammar structures at the B2 level.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: First Conditional Formula for Real Future Possibilities
blueprintItems.formula: If + present simple, will + base verb
blueprintItems.example: If you tell the truth about the missing document, your colleagues will respect you.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Second Conditional Formula for Hypothetical Situations
blueprintItems.formula: If + past simple, would + base verb
blueprintItems.example: If I found a wallet full of money on the street, I would take it to the local police station.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Third Conditional Formula for Past Hypotheses
blueprintItems.formula: If + past perfect, would have + past participle
blueprintItems.example: If Sarah had checked her brakes before the trip, she would not have crashed into the fence.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place a comma after a conditional clause when it begins the sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If you help me with this dilemma I will be grateful.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If you help me with this dilemma, I will be grateful.
mechanicsRules.why: Introductory dependent clauses require a comma before the independent main clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Never use 'would' in the 'if' clause of second conditional sentences.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If she would study harder, she would pass the exam.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If she studied harder, she would pass the exam.
mechanicsRules.why: The condition clause requires the past simple tense, while the result clause takes 'would'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'unless' to mean 'if not' in conditional arguments.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You will not resolve the conflict if you do not talk to him.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: You will not resolve the conflict unless you talk to him.
mechanicsRules.why: Unless streamlines negative conditional sentences effectively at the B2 level.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Dilemmas: First & Second Conditional

content.summary: Mastering conditional structures in spoken English requires precise control over sentence stress, linking, and intonation. When speaking about hypothetical situations using second conditionals, native speakers often reduce auxiliary verbs and link modal verbs to pronouns, creating a smooth rhythm. Clear vowel articulation in conditional clauses prevents ambiguity between real possibilities and imaginary scenarios.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to sentence stress when delivering conditional clauses. In first conditionals, stress both the condition clause and the result clause equally. In second conditionals, stress the modal verb (would, could, might) and the main verb, while compressing the past tense verb in the if clause.

pillars.name: Conditional Rhythm
pillars.target: Balanced pacing in if-clauses and result clauses
pillars.explanation: Native speakers pause slightly after the if-clause before delivering the main result. Practising this natural pause improves clarity.

pillars.name: Modal Reduction
pillars.explanation: In fast, natural speech, 'I would tell the truth' becomes 'I'd tell the truth'. Pronouncing the contraction clearly is essential for B2 fluency.

pillars.name: Intonation Contours
pillars.target: Rising pitch on condition, falling pitch on outcome
pillars.explanation: Use a rising tone at the end of the if-clause to show suspense, and a falling tone on the main clause to signal the final decision.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how primary stress shifts depending on word length and prefix structure.
The root syllable maintains stress when adding grammatical suffixes.
Compound and derived adjectives keep primary stress on the initial root.
In phrasal verbs, both the lexical verb and the particle carry distinct emphasis.
